judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's mathematical claims are exact and I confirmed each independently against the artifacts. Counting the drawn arrays: problem 2 is 3 rows of 6 dots, problem 4 is 4 rows of 7 stars, problem 7 is 6 rows of 4 counters; recomputing the sheet gives 20, 18, 21, 28 (and 28 read down the columns), 18, 6, 24, 30, 7, 24, 30, and the challenge rows 4 and 8 — identical to the judge's list, and identical to verify.json's fourteen entries. Where I part company is instruction_following at 4/4. The prompt ends 'clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review', and verify.json contains no entry of type manual (machine_observation confirms gate_chain_manual_flags: false) while the worksheet prints four responses that are not machine-checkable: problem 6 'Fill in the missing factor, then say how you know', problem 10 'Explain what Ben mixed up, write 4 x 6 as a repeated addition, and give the correct product', problem 11 part (a) 'How many rows are there now?' (answer 5, which no verify entry computes — id 11's only entry is (a+1)*b = 30, part (b)), and problem 12 part (b) 'Write the repeated addition that matches that array'. final_response.md states the position explicitly: 'Nothing is flagged for manual review — every problem on this sheet has a machine-checkable answer', two sentences before conceding 'Problem 10 and problem 12(b) also ask the child to write an explanation or a repeated addition'. That concession is the defect stated in the author's own words. The judge did not test that clause of the prompt, so its 32/32 is not wrong about the mathematics — it is silent about the verification contract.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 4 is verified TWICE from one figure: verify.json carries two id-4 entries, expr 'a*b' (4 rows of 7) and expr 'b*a' (7 columns of 4), both expected 28, and the answer key prints both readings as separate boxed answers with the line 'an array can be read two ways, which is exactly why 4 x 7 and 7 x 4 are equal. Not a rule to memorise — a picture to turn.' This is the right way to make commutativity checkable instead of asserted; keep the pattern of one figure carrying two bound checks.

The interleave is real, not nominal: after the two warm-ups the facet sequence runs repeated-addition, array, product-to-addition, missing-factor, array, repeated-addition, missing-factor, product-to-addition, array, missing-factor, so no facet runs more than twice and the child must choose a method at every problem.

Problem 10's planted error is declared as a trap with expr 'a + b', value 10, so the wrong answer is machine-proved to be distinguishable from 24, and it prints in the key's 'Common wrong answers' block rather than as a boxed answer.

The study guide covers all four facets in four boxes, each with a rule in plain language, a worked example whose first step says why the method fits, and a distinct re-parameterised try-it (rule 4+4+4, example 3x4, try-it 5+5+5+5), plus a closing watch-out that names this topic's real error: 4 x 6 is not 4 + 6.

root_causes.description: Items whose response is an explanation are recorded with an ordinary machine-verified type instead of carrying a companion 'manual' entry. SKILL.md line 249 already reserves 'manual' for 'genuinely open reasoning (proofs, "explain why", construction)', but nothing in the gate chain detects an 'Explain'/'say how you know' stem, so the build reports all-green with zero manual items and the delivery text then asserts that nothing needs human review.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 10: 'Explain what Ben mixed up, write 4 x 6 as a repeated addition, and give the correct product.' verify.json id 10 is a single {"type": "eval", "expr": "a*b", "expected": 24} entry.
worksheet.pdf problem 6: 'Fill in the missing factor, then say how you know.' verify.json id 6 is a single {"type": "solve", "expr": "4*x - 24", "expected": [6]} entry.
verify.json contains no entry with "type": "manual"; the packet's machine_observation records gate_chain_manual_flags: false.
final_response.md: 'Nothing is flagged for manual review — every problem on this sheet has a machine-checkable answer, which is what the "machine first" setting asks for.'

root_causes.description: A problem may print more answer blanks than its verify entries supply expected values, and no gate compares the two. tests/check_layout.py only requires that AT LEAST ONE answer-location macro exists per item (and exempts \problem regions entirely, since the macro emits its own line), so a multi-part item whose parts have separate answers can ship with one part unchecked.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 11 prints '(a) How many rows are there now?' and '(b) How many tiles are there altogether?'; verify.json id 11 has one entry, (a + 1)*b = 30, which is part (b) only. The value 5 for part (a) exists nowhere in verify.json.
worksheet.pdf problem 12 prints three parts (a) rows, (b) the repeated addition, (c) rows of 4; verify.json id 12 has two entries, 8*x - 32 = 4 and 4*x - 32 = 8, covering (a) and (c) only.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers prints '11. 30' and '12. 4, 8' — a grader marking from the bank has no printed value for 11(a) or 12(b).
tests/check_layout.py line 399: the answer-location rule fires only when a region has NO answer macro ('items {noans} have no designated answer location'), never on a count mismatch.

improvements.title: Gate the worksheet stem for explanation verbs and require a companion manual entry
improvements.proposed_change: Extend tests/check_answer_line.py (it already receives both the worksheet .tex and verify.json, and is already wired as build.sh gate 10 'answer-line-ws') with an open-response scan. Segment the sheet with _tex_segments.segment_spans, and for each problem region match a closed lexicon of open-response imperatives against the stem — 'explain', 'why', 'in your own words', 'say how you know', 'what do you notice', 'describe', 'tell', 'draw', 'sketch', 'circle', 'mark', 'of your own choosing'. If a region matches and that id has no entry with "type": "manual", exit 1 with the problem number, the matched phrase and the exact JSON entry to add. Mirror the rule in SKILL.md step 4 next to the existing sentence 'Reserve manual for genuinely open reasoning', so the instruction and the gate say the same thing. For curr-070 specifically, ids 6 and 10 each need a manual companion alongside their existing check, which turns the build into a clean exit 2 and makes final_response.md say 'two items flagged for manual review' instead of 'nothing'.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/fixtures/open_response_unflagged/ holding a two-problem worksheet whose problem 2 stem reads 'Explain what Ben mixed up, then give the correct product.' and a verify.json whose id 2 is a lone {"type": "eval", "expr": "a*b", "at": {"a": 4, "b": 6}, "expected": 24}. Assert check_answer_line.py exits 1 and its stderr names problem 2 and the word 'Explain'. Append {"id": 2, "type": "manual", "desc": "..."} to the fixture's verify.json and assert the same invocation exits 0. Both directions must be asserted — an exit-1-only test passes against a gate that fails everything.
improvements.expected_impact: The 36-case cluster behind this key stops shipping as all-green machine-verified. Concretely for curr-070, the grader learns that problem 6's justification and problem 10's diagnosis are theirs to read, and the delivery text can no longer claim complete machine coverage while the sheet asks a child to write a sentence.
improvements.risk: A lexicon over natural-language stems will false-positive on incidental uses ('explain' inside a teaching note, 'circle' as a shape noun in a geometry sheet). Mitigate by scanning only the student-facing stem text (comments blanked, \emph and \textbf stripped) and by making the message a fix instruction rather than a mystery, so an author facing a genuine false positive declares the manual entry in one line rather than hunting the gate. Keep the lexicon closed and version it, as tests/_units.py does for units.

improvements.title: Fail the build when a problem prints more answer blanks than its verify entries cover
improvements.proposed_change: In tests/check_answer_line.py, count the answer-location macros in each problem region (\ansline, \ansblank, \answerline, plus the one line the \problem macro emits when its workspace argument is positive) and compare that count with the number of verify.json entries for the same id that carry either an 'expected' value or "type": "manual". When the blanks outnumber the covered slots, exit 1 naming the problem, the counts, and the two remedies: add the missing entry, or merge the parts into one answer line. Document the rule in SKILL.md's JSON-format section beside the existing sentence that every id 1..N needs at least one check — the contract becomes 'at least one check PER PRINTED SLOT', not per problem.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/fixtures/slot_undercount/ with a worksheet whose problem 1 prints two \ansblank ('(a) How many rows are there now?~\ansblank (b) How many tiles altogether?~\ansblank') against a verify.json carrying one id-1 entry (expected 30). Assert check_answer_line.py exits 1 and reports '2 printed answer slots, 1 covered'. Add the second entry ({"id": 1, "type": "eval", "expr": "a + 1", "at": {"a": 4}, "expected": 5}) and assert exit 0.
improvements.expected_impact: Closes the largest verification hole in the run (61 cases). For curr-070 it forces entries for problem 11(a)'s row count and problem 12(b)'s repeated addition, so the Quick Answers bank prints every value a child is asked to write.
improvements.risk: Sheets that use an inline blank as scaffolding rather than as a graded answer (a partially completed equation the student finishes on the way to the real answer) will now fail. That is mostly the point, but it will force authors either to declare the scaffold value or to switch it to a non-answer rule; provide the second option explicitly in the failure message so the fix is not always 'add JSON'.

case_summary: A genuinely strong grade 2-3 multiplication-foundations sheet that earns its ACCEPT on content. I recomputed all fourteen checks and re-counted every drawn array against the .tex coordinates: problem 2 is 3 rows of 6, problem 4 is 4 rows of 7, problem 7 is 6 rows of 4, and each printed total matches both the picture and verify.json. The interleave after the two warm-ups is real (no facet runs more than twice), problem 4 turns one array into two bound checks, and the study guide gives all four facets a rule, a worked example and a distinct try-it inside two pages. The defect is not in the mathematics but in the verification contract. Four printed responses — problem 6's 'say how you know', problem 10's 'Explain what Ben mixed up', problem 11(a)'s row count and problem 12(b)'s repeated addition — have no verify entry of their own, and none is declared manual, so the build finished all-green with zero manual flags and final_response.md told the parent that nothing needs a human read on a sheet that asks a seven-year-old to explain a classmate's error. Both remedies are mechanical: a stem scan that requires a manual companion for explanation verbs, and a slot count that requires one covered check per printed blank. Neither changes a single number on this worksheet.
